questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A man with hepatitis C and iron overload has blistering and fragile skin on the backs of his hands with hypertrichosis, and pink fluorescent urine. Which enzyme is deficient?
options: Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase, giving porphyria cutanea tarda
questions.concept: It is the commonest porphyria, is usually acquired with hepatitis C, alcohol or iron as triggers, and responds to venesection or low-dose hydroxychloroquine rather than to the haem infusion used for acute attacks.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Haemoglobin and Porphyrins

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A child develops immediate burning and swelling of sun-exposed skin without blistering, and red cell protoporphyrin is markedly raised. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.concept: The terminal step inserting ferrous iron into protoporphyrin IX fails, so the accumulated photoreactive porphyrin causes acute painful photosensitivity, and liver disease from protoporphyrin deposition is the serious complication.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Haemoglobin and Porphyrins

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes Crigler-Najjar type II from type I?
options: Type II has no enzyme activity at all
Type II retains partial glucuronyl transferase activity and responds to phenobarbitone
Type II presents with conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia
Type II is acquired rather than inherited
questions.concept: Because the enzyme is inducible in type II the bilirubin falls with an enzyme inducer, whereas type I has absent activity, does not respond, and requires phototherapy and ultimately liver transplantation to prevent kernicterus.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Haemoglobin and Porphyrins

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A young man has mild fluctuating unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia that rises with fasting or illness, with normal liver enzymes and no haemolysis. What is the diagnosis?
questions.concept: Reduced glucuronyl transferase activity of about 30 percent explains it, the condition is benign and needs no treatment, and its main importance is avoiding unnecessary investigation and predicting irinotecan toxicity.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Haemoglobin and Porphyrins

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes Rotor syndrome from Dubin-Johnson syndrome?
options: In Rotor syndrome the liver is not pigmented and gallbladder visualisation on cholecystography is normal
Rotor syndrome is associated with a black liver
questions.concept: Both cause benign conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia from defective canalicular excretion, but the dense melanin-like pigment and the non-visualised gallbladder belong to Dubin-Johnson syndrome.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Haemoglobin and Porphyrins

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the cellular compartments used in haem synthesis?
options: The whole pathway occurs in the cytosol
The whole pathway occurs in mitochondria
The first and the last three steps occur in mitochondria while the intermediate steps occur in the cytosol
Only the final step occurs in the cytosol
questions.concept: This shuttling means the pathway needs succinyl-CoA from the citric acid cycle to begin, and mitochondrial disease or lead, which inhibits both cytosolic ALA dehydratase and mitochondrial ferrochelatase, disrupts it at more than one point.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Haemoglobin and Porphyrins

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Why does unconjugated rather than conjugated bilirubin cause kernicterus in a neonate?
options: Unconjugated bilirubin is lipid soluble and, when it exceeds albumin binding capacity, crosses the immature blood-brain barrier
Conjugated bilirubin is more lipid soluble
Unconjugated bilirubin is actively transported into neurons
Conjugated bilirubin binds albumin more weakly
questions.concept: This is why acidosis, hypoalbuminaemia, sepsis and drugs that displace bilirubin from albumin such as sulphonamides and ceftriaxone lower the threshold at which exchange transfusion becomes necessary.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Haemoglobin and Porphyrins

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which group of drugs can precipitate an acute attack of intermittent porphyria and why?
options: Barbiturates and other cytochrome P450 inducers, because induction increases haem demand and de-represses ALA synthase
Beta blockers, by reducing hepatic blood flow
questions.concept: Fasting, infection and hormonal fluctuation act by the same final route, so avoiding porphyrinogenic drugs and giving carbohydrate and haem arginate together suppress the overactive first step.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Haemoglobin and Porphyrins

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.topic: Integration of metabolism: fed/fasting, diabetes, ketosis
questions.stem: Which regulatory step explains why fatty acids are oxidised rather than synthesised during fasting?
options: Malonyl-CoA falls, releasing inhibition of carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 so fatty acids enter the mitochondrion
Acetyl-CoA carboxylase is activated by glucagon
Hormone-sensitive lipase is inhibited by adrenaline
questions.concept: The same molecule that commits carbon to synthesis also blocks its oxidation, so this single switch prevents a futile cycle and explains why insulin favours storage and glucagon favours oxidation.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry 32e, Ch. Metabolic Integration

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.topic: Integration of metabolism: fed/fasting, diabetes, ketosis
questions.stem: What is the respiratory quotient for the complete oxidation of carbohydrate compared with that of fat?
options: 1.0 for carbohydrate and about 0.7 for fat
questions.concept: Fat is more reduced so it consumes more oxygen per carbon dioxide produced, and a value above 1.0 indicates net lipogenesis, which is why overfeeding a ventilated patient increases the carbon dioxide load.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry 32e, Ch. Metabolic Integration

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.topic: Integration of metabolism: fed/fasting, diabetes, ketosis
questions.stem: Roughly how long do hepatic glycogen stores maintain blood glucose during a fast, and what takes over?
options: About 24 hours, after which gluconeogenesis predominates
About 7 days, after which ketogenesis begins
About 2 hours, after which muscle glycogen is used
About 3 days, after which protein breakdown begins
questions.concept: Liver glycogen is limited to roughly 100 grams whereas adipose triacylglycerol holds many days of energy, and muscle glycogen cannot contribute directly because muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry 32e, Ch. Metabolic Integration

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.topic: Integration of metabolism: fed/fasting, diabetes, ketosis
questions.stem: Why can the liver synthesise ketone bodies but not use them as fuel?
options: It lacks succinyl-CoA acetoacetate transferase, the thiophorase needed to activate acetoacetate
questions.concept: This compartmentalisation guarantees that the ketone bodies made in the liver are exported for use by brain, heart and skeletal muscle rather than consumed at the site of production.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry 32e, Ch. Metabolic Integration

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.topic: Integration of metabolism: fed/fasting, diabetes, ketosis
questions.stem: Which cycle transfers both carbon and nitrogen from muscle to liver during fasting?
options: The Cori cycle, transferring lactate only
The glucose-alanine cycle, in which alanine carries the amino nitrogen for ureagenesis and the carbon skeleton for gluconeogenesis
questions.concept: Muscle transaminates pyruvate to alanine because it cannot make urea, so the liver receives a substrate that serves gluconeogenesis and nitrogen disposal at the same time.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry 32e, Ch. Metabolic Integration

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.topic: Integration of metabolism: fed/fasting, diabetes, ketosis
questions.stem: A severely malnourished patient develops weakness, arrhythmia and a falling serum phosphate 3 days after starting nutritional support. What has happened?
options: Refeeding syndrome, in which the insulin surge drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells
questions.concept: Depleted intracellular stores are unmasked when anabolism resumes, so feeding is introduced slowly with thiamine before calories and with daily electrolyte monitoring during the first week.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry 32e, Ch. Metabolic Integration

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.topic: Integration of metabolism: fed/fasting, diabetes, ketosis
questions.stem: Which single metabolite reciprocally activates glycolysis and inhibits gluconeogenesis in the liver?
questions.concept: Insulin raises it and glucagon lowers it through a bifunctional enzyme, so one molecule sets the direction of hepatic glucose handling and prevents the two opposing pathways running at once.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry 32e, Ch. Metabolic Integration

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.topic: Integration of metabolism: fed/fasting, diabetes, ketosis
questions.stem: What is meant by the protein-sparing effect of dietary carbohydrate?
options: Adequate carbohydrate suppresses gluconeogenesis from amino acids so body protein is preserved
Carbohydrate is converted directly into protein
questions.concept: This is why a minimum carbohydrate intake matters in the management of protein-energy malnutrition and why the negative nitrogen balance of starvation is corrected by energy before extra protein.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry 32e, Ch. Metabolic Integration

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Deficiency of which trace element impairs glutathione peroxidase and causes an endemic cardiomyopathy?
questions.concept: The element sits in the enzyme as selenocysteine, so deficiency leaves cells vulnerable to peroxide injury, and Kashin-Beck osteoarthropathy is the skeletal counterpart of the same deficiency.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Minerals and Acid-Base Balance

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A neonate has intractable seizures, lens dislocation and raised urinary sulphite. Deficiency of which trace element cofactor explains this?
questions.concept: The same cofactor is needed by xanthine oxidase and aldehyde oxidase, so urate is characteristically low, and the combination of low urate with high sulphite points to the cofactor rather than to a single enzyme defect.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Minerals and Acid-Base Balance

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which trace element is required for normal insulin action and glucose tolerance?
questions.concept: Deficiency has been described in long-term parenteral nutrition without supplementation, producing glucose intolerance and peripheral neuropathy that reverse when the element is replaced.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Minerals and Acid-Base Balance

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which protein regulates iron absorption, and how is it altered in hereditary haemochromatosis?
options: Hepcidin, which is inappropriately low so ferroportin remains active and absorption continues
questions.concept: Hepcidin normally degrades ferroportin to shut off absorption when stores are full, so its failure explains the progressive overload, and in anaemia of inflammation the opposite occurs with high hepcidin trapping iron in macrophages.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Minerals and Acid-Base Balance

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A patient has a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis. Which measurement distinguishes renal tubular acidosis from gastrointestinal bicarbonate loss?
options: The urinary anion gap, which is positive in renal tubular acidosis and negative with diarrhoea
questions.concept: A negative value reflects the large ammonium excretion of an appropriately responding kidney, so its absence indicates that the defect in acid handling lies in the kidney itself.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Minerals and Acid-Base Balance

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A patient with severe metabolic acidosis has a measured serum osmolality 30 mOsm above the calculated value. Which poisoning does this suggest?
questions.concept: The parent alcohol is osmotically active before it is metabolised, so an early osmolar gap with a later widening anion gap is the classic sequence, and fomepizole or ethanol blocks alcohol dehydrogenase to prevent formation of the toxic acid metabolites.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Minerals and Acid-Base Balance

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Why is the bicarbonate system the most effective extracellular buffer despite a pKa of 6.1, well away from blood pH?
options: It has an unusually high buffering capacity per molecule
It is an open system in which carbon dioxide is continuously removed by the lungs and bicarbonate regulated by the kidney
It is present at higher concentration than any intracellular buffer
Its pKa shifts to 7.4 in plasma
questions.concept: A closed buffer would be nearly exhausted at this distance from its pKa, so it is the physiological regulation of both components rather than the chemistry alone that gives the system its power.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Minerals and Acid-Base Balance

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which role does phosphate play in renal acid excretion?
options: It acts as titratable acid, accepting a proton in the tubular fluid to allow net acid excretion
It is reabsorbed in exchange for bicarbonate
It buffers only in the interstitium
It is the main urinary buffer at all urine pH values
questions.concept: Ammonium excretion is the larger and more adaptable component, increasing several fold in chronic acidosis, whereas titratable acid is limited by the amount of phosphate filtered.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Minerals and Acid-Base Balance

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which enzyme does 5-fluorouracil inhibit, and what is the consequence?
options: Thymidylate synthase, so dTMP cannot be made and DNA synthesis fails
questions.concept: Its active metabolite forms a stable complex with the enzyme and its folate cofactor, which is why leucovorin potentiates rather than rescues from fluorouracil, in contrast to its use after methotrexate.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Nucleotide Metabolism

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A patient develops profound myelosuppression soon after starting azathioprine. Which enzyme polymorphism explains this?
options: Low thiopurine methyltransferase activity, so more drug is shunted to active thioguanine nucleotides
questions.concept: Testing activity or genotype before treatment identifies those needing a reduced dose, and coprescribing allopurinol is hazardous because blocking the other catabolic route diverts still more drug to the cytotoxic pathway.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Nucleotide Metabolism

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: How does probenecid lower serum urate, and when is it inappropriate?
options: It inhibits xanthine oxidase, and is inappropriate in renal failure
It blocks urate reabsorption in the proximal tubule, and is inappropriate in urate overproduction or a history of urate stones
It converts urate to allantoin, and is inappropriate in G6PD deficiency
It alkalinises the urine, and is inappropriate in hypertension
questions.concept: Increasing urinary urate excretion risks crystallisation in the tubules, so a xanthine oxidase inhibitor is preferred when the 24-hour urinary urate is already high or stones have occurred.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Nucleotide Metabolism

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which agent is used to prevent tumour lysis nephropathy in a child with a high leukaemic burden, and by what mechanism?
options: Rasburicase, a recombinant urate oxidase that converts urate to soluble allantoin
Allopurinol, which converts urate to allantoin
questions.concept: Humans lack urate oxidase, so supplying it bypasses the least soluble end product entirely, and it is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency because the hydrogen peroxide generated causes haemolysis.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Nucleotide Metabolism

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Why does a complete block in pyrimidine catabolism cause less clinical harm than one in purine catabolism?
options: Pyrimidines are not catabolised in humans
Pyrimidine degradation yields highly water-soluble products such as beta-alanine and ammonia, whereas purine degradation ends in poorly soluble urate
Pyrimidines are excreted unchanged in bile
questions.concept: This solubility difference is the reason gout is a purine disorder, and it also explains why disorders of pyrimidine catabolism present with neurological or drug-toxicity phenotypes rather than with crystal deposition.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Nucleotide Metabolism

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which molecule is the common activated precursor for purine synthesis, pyrimidine synthesis and NAD salvage?
questions.concept: Its central position explains why the enzyme that makes it is a key regulatory point, and why superactivity of that enzyme causes purine overproduction with gout in childhood.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Nucleotide Metabolism

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Why do alcohol excess and lactic acidosis precipitate an acute attack of gout?
options: They increase de novo purine synthesis directly
Organic acids compete with urate for tubular secretion, so urate excretion falls
questions.concept: Low-dose aspirin, thiazides and ketoacidosis act by the same competition at the tubular transporter, whereas beer also adds a purine load, so alcohol raises urate by two routes at once.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Nucleotide Metabolism

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: How does colchicine relieve an acute attack of gout?
options: It binds tubulin and prevents microtubule assembly, so neutrophil migration and inflammasome activation are inhibited
It dissolves urate crystals in the joint
questions.concept: Because it does not alter urate it neither treats nor worsens the underlying hyperuricaemia, and its narrow margin with diarrhoea as the dose-limiting effect is why it is given in low dose.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Nucleotide Metabolism
